About: limb darkening: a slanting line of sight sees higher, cooler layers of a grey atmosphere

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the star from the side, radius R, centre marked, a horizontal line of sight leaving the surface at height b, the radius to the exit point continued as a dashed normal, and the angle θ between normal and line of sight. Right, at the same heights: the face of the star on a dark sky, painted ring by ring with the brightness I(θ)/I(0) and blackbody colour of each swept line of sight. Below: I(θ)/I(0) against b/R where you have swept, and, when there is room, a column of the atmosphere from its top (τ = 0) downwards, shaded by the light each layer emits, with the layer the line of sight reaches marked. The atmosphere is far thinner than the drawn outline suggests.
Controls
The impact parameter b/R moves the line of sight from the disc centre (0) to the limb (1); rings stay painted as you sweep. The chips jump to the values the questions use. Clear the face wipes the painted rings.
Measured
θ from sin θ = b/R; the layer seen is at vertical optical depth τ = cos θ (Eddington–Barbier); its temperature from the grey-atmosphere law with Teff = 5772 K; I(θ)/I(0) relative to the disc centre, never renormalised.
Model limits
The atmosphere is plane-parallel and grey: its opacity is the same at every wavelength, so the brightness shown is the total over all wavelengths, which for the Sun is close to this model. The real Sun darkens more towards the limb in blue light and less in red light.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Across the face of the star

Set the impact parameter to b/R = 0, so that the line of sight passes through the centre of the disc. Before sliding it outwards, predict how the brightness of the face of the star will change from the centre to the edge.

2 · How deep we see

Set b/R = 0.5, and watch the readout of the optical depth τ of the layer that is seen. Before moving to b/R = 0.9, predict how deep into the atmosphere the line of sight will reach there.

3 · Why the edge looks darker

Keep b/R = 0.9. Before looking at the temperature readout, predict why the face of the star is darker at this line of sight than at the centre.

4 · The layer at two thirds

Set b/R = 0.745, where the layer that is seen has τ = 2/3. Before reading its temperature, predict how it compares with the effective temperature of the star, 5772 K.

5 · Brightness at the limb

Slide the line of sight all the way to the limb, b/R = 1. Before looking at the inset, predict the brightness there as a fraction of the brightness at the centre.

6 · Why the limb is dark

Every line of sight sees down to about one unit of optical depth along its own path. Near the limb the path is slanted, so it reaches that depth higher in the atmosphere, at τ = cos θ, where the gas is cooler.

Cooler gas emits less, so the face darkens from the centre to 2/5 at the edge, and the layer at τ = 2/3 has the effective temperature.

Limb darkening is direct evidence that the temperature of a star's atmosphere falls outwards: an atmosphere at one temperature would look uniformly bright.

01

At a glance

This sim follows a single line of sight across the face of a star. You choose where the line crosses the disc, and the sim shows the layer of the atmosphere it reaches, that layer's temperature and its brightness.

What you'll learn

  • How the angle at which a line of sight leaves the star follows from where it crosses the disc.
  • How the layer it reaches, and that layer's temperature, depend on the angle.
  • How the brightness I(θ)/I(0) is built from that layer.
The stage: the star from the side with a line of sight at height b, and the same star face on.

What's on screen

  • Cyan line: the line of sight, with pulses of light moving along it. The dashed line is the normal to the surface where it leaves.
  • Face on, right: painted ring by ring as you sweep b/R.
  • Plot, bottom left: I(θ)/I(0) against b/R where you have swept. Column, bottom right: the atmosphere from its top (τ = 0) downwards, with the layer reached marked in cyan and τ = 2/3 in amber.
See itLook at the stage with the opening settings. Watch for: the cyan line running along the radius through the centre, a dot at the centre of the blank face, and θ = 0.0° in the readouts.

03

Where the line of sight leaves the star

A line of sight is a straight ray from the star to the observer. Its impact parameter b is its distance from the axis through the centre, and R is the radius of the star. Where the ray leaves the surface it makes an angle θ with the outward normal, the radius continued outwards (notes, Fig. 35a). The right-angled triangle in the figure gives:

sin θ = b / R
b/R = 0 is the disc centre, with θ = 0°. b/R = 1 is the limb, with θ = 90°.
The geometry, drawn for b/R = 0.6, where θ = 36.9°.

The atmosphere is a thin skin on the surface, far thinner than the drawn outline suggests. Its depth is measured by the optical depth τ: τ = 0 at the top, larger τ deeper in, and light travelling straight out from depth τ is dimmed by a factor e−τ.

See itMove the line of sight from the centre out to b/R = 0.5. Watch for: the cyan line rising above the axis, and θ reaching 30.0°, as sin 30° = 0.5.
04

A slanted line of sight reaches a higher layer

The light you receive comes from about one unit of optical depth back along the line of sight: gas farther in is hidden by the gas in front of it. A ray leaving at angle θ crosses each layer along a path longer by 1/cos θ, so it uses up that unit sooner. In vertical depth it reaches only (Eddington–Barbier, notes §3.4):

τ = cos θ
The layer seen by a line of sight that leaves at angle θ. The sim's τ readout.
Two rays, to scale, each with one unit of optical depth along its own path. The slanted one starts at τ = cos θ = 0.436.

At the centre θ = 0° and τ = 1. At b/R = 0.5, θ = 30° and τ = 0.866. At b/R = 0.9, θ = 64.2° and τ = 0.436. As b/R → 1, θ → 90° and τ → 0, the top of the atmosphere.

Key idea. Near the limb the line of sight cuts the atmosphere at a shallow angle, so one unit of optical depth along the path lies high in the atmosphere.
See itSweep the line of sight from the centre out to b/R = 0.9. Watch for: τ falling from 1.000 to 0.436 in the readouts, and the cyan mark in the atmosphere column rising towards the top.
05

The layer seen is cooler near the limb

In the grey atmosphere, in the Eddington approximation, the temperature rises with depth (notes, 3.40):

T4 = ¾ Teff4 (τ + 2/3)
Equation (3.40). Teff = 5772 K in the sim.

At the centre τ = 1 and T = 6103 K. At b/R = 0.9, τ = 0.436 and T = 5504 K. At the top τ = 0 and T = 2−1/4 Teff = 4854 K, the coolest layer. The source function of this atmosphere is S = σSBT4/π, so a cooler layer emits less.

The temperature of the layer against τ. The cyan points are the layers seen at b/R = 0, 0.9 and 1.
b/R

This slider moves the sim too. The numbers use the sim's own formulas.

See itStart at the centre, then move the line of sight out to b/R = 0.9. Watch for: the temperature readout falling from 6103 K to 5504 K as the layer seen moves up.
06

The layer at τ = 2/3 has the effective temperature

Putting τ = 2/3 into (3.40) gives T = Teff exactly. The flux leaving the star is that of a blackbody at the temperature of this layer, F = πS(τ = 2/3) = σSBTeff4 (notes, 3.41). This is why the layer near τ = 2/3 is called the photosphere.

T(τ = 2/3) = Teff

Setting cos θ = 2/3 gives b/R = sin θ = √(1 − 4/9) = √5/3 = 0.745, with θ = 48.2°. There T = 5772 K, the effective temperature, and I(θ)/I(0) = 0.800.

Key idea. The effective temperature of a star is the temperature of the layer seen at b/R = 0.745.
See itSweep the line of sight from the centre out to b/R = 0.745. Watch for: the temperature readout falling to 5772 K and the cyan mark meeting the amber dashed line at τ = 2/3 in the column.
07

Brightness falls to 2/5 of the centre value at the limb

By the Eddington–Barbier relation the specific intensity along a line of sight is the source function at τ = cos θ. For this atmosphere that is S0 + S1 cos θ, with S0 = σSBTeff4/2π and S1 = 3σSBTeff4/4π, so (notes, 3.42):

I(θ) / I(0) = (S0 + S1 cos θ) / (S0 + S1) = (2 + 3 cos θ) / 5
Equation (3.42). The sim never renormalises: the centre is 1 by definition.

The values are 0.920 at b/R = 0.5, 0.800 at 0.745, 0.662 at 0.9 and 0.400 at the limb. The fall is gentle at first, 8% by half the radius, and steeper near the edge. At the limb the top of the atmosphere, at 4854 K, still glows: the face is dimmer there, not dark.

The brightness across the disc, from equation (3.42).
See itSweep the line of sight from the centre all the way to the limb. Watch for: I(θ)/I(0) falling slowly at first and faster near the end, to 0.400 and not to zero, with the face painted ring by ring.
08

Where it matters

  • The Sun. Photographs show its disc darker towards the limb. The model's 2/5 at the limb agrees fairly well with the darkening measured in visible light (notes, 3.4).
  • Colour. The measured darkening is stronger at shorter wavelengths: on the short-wavelength side of its peak the Planck function rises steeply with T, so the cooler layers near the limb lose more there. The limb looks redder than the centre. The face's tint shows this, since each ring takes the blackbody colour of the cooler layer seen there; but the brightness curve is the total over all wavelengths, so it cannot show the stronger darkening in blue light.
  • Other stars. Limb darkening can be measured from the shapes of the eclipses of eclipsing binaries (notes, 2.2).
09

Summary

In one line. Each line of sight reports on one layer of the atmosphere, and which layer depends on where it crosses the disc.
  • sin θ = b/R, and the layer seen is at τ = cos θ.
  • T4 = ¾ Teff4 (τ + 2/3): T = Teff at τ = 2/3 (b/R = 0.745), and 4854 K at the top.
  • I(θ)/I(0) = (2 + 3 cos θ)/5, which is 2/5 at the limb.

Common mix-ups

  • "Every part of the surface is at the same temperature, so the disc is uniform." Different lines of sight reach different layers, at different temperatures.
  • "A longer path through glowing gas should brighten the limb." You see only about one unit of optical depth along the path, and a slanted path ends higher up.
  • "At the limb the brightness drops to zero." The top of the atmosphere still glows: I = 2/5 of the centre value at the limb.

Things to try on your own

  • Set b/R = 0.745. T should read 5772 K and I(θ)/I(0) should read 0.800.
  • Press Clear the face, then sweep slowly from 0 to 1.
  • Find the b/R where I(θ)/I(0) reads 0.500: about 0.986.
